thread.title: Dialog Semiconductor Plc: Distilling Risk From Uncertainty - Dialog Semiconductor Plc (OTCMKTS:DLGNF)

author: Oyat
title: Dialog Semiconductor Plc: Distilling Risk From Uncertainty - Dialog Semiconductor Plc (OTCMKTS:DLGNF)
text:
A prospective investment in Dialog Semiconductor Plc ( OTCPK:DLGNF ) is not for the faint-hearted. Most investors would perhaps rightly decline the opportunity based on the single fact that the company derived over 3/4th of sales from its main customer, Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ), in 2017. Having said that, one might reasonably argue that as far as the stock price is concerned, this customer concentration risk has essentially been realized, at least to some extent. So, what is the risk of permanent capital impairment, and what might a prospective return on investment look like from today’s stock price? These are the main questions this article aims to answer.
Company background and description Before we dive into it, just a bit of background about the firm. Dialog is a semiconductor company focused on the development of mixed-signal integrated circuits (ICs).
Its origins go back to the European operations of International Microelectronic Products, Inc., a Silicon Valley company founded in 1981. Dialog was then formed as part of Messerschmitt-Bölkow-Blohm (now part of Daimler-Benz) in 1989. A decade later, Dialog Semiconductor plc formed, and the company was listed on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange in 1999.
What does Dialog do? It primarily develops power management ICs for consumer electronics such as mobile phones. Noteworthy innovations include the world’s first configurable power management IC in 2009, the development of audio codecs, as well as 2D-3D image conversion ICs for portable devices. Dialog Semiconductor is "fabless" (i.e., it outsources manufacturing, mainly to TSMC), but it maintains its own test laboratories.

Fundamental profile Before looking at the crux of the matter, let’s briefly review the firm’s underlying fundamentals and make sure that it is indeed an investment worthy of consideration.
So, we’re talking about a company operating in the US$ 400 billion+ global semiconductor market, which has been growing at a CAGR of approx. 5-6% over the past 20 years. It specializes in the relatively small sub-segment of mixed-signal ICs. These are vital components for applications in consumer electronics, automotive, and IoT, amongst others, as they are necessary to process analog signals such as temperature, pressure, light, weight, and sound within digitally-based operating systems. Some of Dialog’s key competitors include established players such as NXP Semiconductors (NASDAQ: NXPI ), Texas Instruments (NYSE: TXN ), Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO ), Renesas Electronics ( OTCPK:RNECF ), and Analog Devices (NASDAQ: ADI ).
As shown below, Dialog has grown at an impressive rate over the past decade, albeit from a small base. Much of that growth has been achieved by being a key supplier to fast-growing Apple. Its profitability levels have steadily increased to reach industry averages, despite the company’s lack of relative scale. Return metrics are entirely satisfactory and easily clear our hurdle rates. Earnings quality is high, and the company generates ample cash flows from operations. Last, Dialog is in a very strong financial position, with close to no debt and over 50% of its current market capitalization in cash and equivalents. In short, we would argue that the company is an asset worth owning, provided it can be acquired at the right price.
(Source: Thomson Reuters Eikon. Data as of end of FY17)
Valuation We looked at 3 different scenarios, detailed below.
Bear case: Dialog get completely cut out of Apple’s supply chain by 2020.
In this very pessimistic scenario, we assume that Dialog gets entirely phased out of Apple’s supply chain by 2020. This leads to a 70%+ cumulative decline in revenues from 2017 to 2020, with the company swinging to a loss during the 2020-2021 period as it scrambles to adjust its cost base. Profitability levels gradually recover in the mid-single digits.
Base case: Apple moves to dual-sourcing for power management ICs for all iPhone launches by 2020.
The highest-probability scenario, in our view, is that Apple will move to dual-source power management ICs for all of its iPhones by 2020. No company wants to be entirely reliant on a single entity to source key components for its products, especially if it has in-house capabilities to mitigate that risk. This would lead to a 35% cumulative decline in revenues from 2017 to 2020. Profitability levels would take a hit, but operating margins would stabilize in the low teens.
Bull case: Status quo. Apple makes no further moves to in-source power management ICs.
Last, we look at a scenario where Apple makes no further reductions in volumes attributed to Dialog. The cumulative decline in revenues from 2017 to 2020 would only amount to about 14%, and profitability levels also decline in the low teens as the company maintains high R&D spending to accelerate growth in areas other than mobile devices, such as connectivity and IoT applications.
The valuation of all 3 scenarios is based on discounted free cash flows, using a WACC of 10% and a terminal growth rate of 2%.

In sum, according to our modelling assumptions, the current market price of about EUR 15 reflects our base case scenario of Apple moving to dual-sourcing for all of its iPhones, but is far from being as bearish as Dialog being entirely cut out of its supply chain.
Other risks to bear in mind Beyond the dependency on Apple and mobile phones as a predominant source of revenue, here are some of the main risks to bear in mind when considering a potential investment in Dialog.
Human capital: This refers to the risk of losing key personnel (mainly design engineers), as has reportedly happened in the recent past (i.e., Apple poaching a number of Dialog’s staff).
Return on R&D investments: In 2017, Dialog spent some 20% of sales on R&D investments, a similar level as leading semiconductor companies. As such, these represent large investments that have uncertain prospects of delivering profitable growth.
Acquisition risk: Dialog understandably has a strategy to accelerate a reduction in dependency to mobile devices (and Apple) by pursuing acquisition opportunities. These carry the typical risks of overpaying for an acquisition target, as well as realizing synergies.
Supply chain interruptions: As a fabless semiconductor company, Dialog is heavily reliant on TSMC for the production of its products, which creates a risk of supply chain interruptions.
Foreign exchange: While most revenues and costs are USD-denominated, Dialog is exposed to both the EUR and the GBP. Also, the primary listing is in Germany, and the stock is therefore listed in EUR (the ADR listing is very illiquid and should probably be avoided), which creates an FX translation risk. Having said that, the company does not currently pay a dividend, so US investors who consider investing in the primary listing do not have worry about a withholding tax.
IP protection and infringement: As a company that aims to be highly innovative, Dialog is exposed to the risk of patent infringement. This is somewhat increased by outsourcing the entirety of its production process and one of its main shareholders (see below).
Quality assurance: Quality standards are stringent in all end-markets, and Dialog must ensure that it meets expectations despite not being in control of the actual manufacturing of its products.
Ownership: Last, it is worth noting that about 9% of Dialog’s capital is owned by Tsinghua University (via its subsidiary Tsinghua Holdings Corp. Ltd.), an entity that has ties to the Chinese political establishment. Other large owners include BlackRock, Kleinwort Benson, and Dorval Asset Management.
Initial conclusions Uncertainty about future business prospects is often what creates the kind of risk/return asymmetries that value investors look for, and a stock price decline of over 70% in slightly more than a year has the potential to be a good starting point. For us, an additional requirement is that the underlying company is fundamentally and financially strong. Dialog meets these criteria. Its balance sheet is as strong as it gets, which will provide much-needed flexibility in addressing its current woes. The firm has historically achieved decent profitability and return levels, while generating ample cash flows.
There remains much uncertainty regarding Dialog’s future prospects with Apple. To what extent will Apple continue the trend of insourcing the production of power management ICs for its iPhones? Will it eventually completely cut Dialog out of its supply chain?
Our brief modelling exercise indicates that despite a massive drop in the stock price, the risk of permanent impairment of capital still exists, should a worst-case scenario come to pass. Having said that, we also recognize the potential upside to both our base and bull scenarios, which are arguably conservative.
At the end of the day, a prospective investment in Dialog at today’s price will depend on individual investors’ level of risk tolerance. For us, the required margin of safety is not quite there yet. But a stock price in the low teens would likely tempt us to initiate a position in the firm. Even so, maximum position sizing would remain on the low-end (about 2% of portfolio), and we would aim to build a position in 2-3 installments in order to provide room to accumulate on further weakness.
Thanks for letting us know in the comments below if you have a different take on the situation.
